Continuous physical training can potentially help counteract some of the negative effects of aging on muscle fiber distribution, as observed in studies that have shown an adaptive response in skeletal muscles. This is particularly relevant for individuals who are already engaging in regular exercise and have a good level of cardiovascular fitness.

However, it's essential to note that myoelectric fatigue refers specifically to the reduction in muscle signal strength due to electrical activity patterns during voluntary contractions. While physical training may help improve overall muscular endurance, its effects on myoelectric fatigue alone might be less clear-cut.

The available research suggests that regular exercise can contribute to an adaptive response in skeletal muscles, which may help mitigate some of the age-related changes in muscle fiber distribution. However, more studies are needed to fully understand the relationship between physical training and myoelectric fatigue in older adults.

It's also worth considering that individual differences in fitness level, genetic predispositions, and other factors can influence the effectiveness of exercise in mitigating aging effects on muscle function. As such, it's unlikely that continuous physical training will completely counteract the aging effect on myoelectric fatigue, but rather serve as one aspect of a broader approach to maintaining physical health and reducing age-related decline.

In summary, while there is some evidence suggesting that continuous physical training may have benefits for older adults in terms of muscle fiber adaptation, more research is needed to fully understand its impact on myoelectric fatigue specifically.
